title: Rules everywhere
hookLine: the Sikh rahit, the Buddhist precepts, Franklin's virtues: ways of life written down so you can see where you stand
tomorrow: God takes his people to court, with mountains for a jury. the verdict?

lines: A BLACK SPOT FOR EACH SLIP.
cards: The black dots were his faults. Benjamin Franklin tells it in his autobiography. He wanted to live without a single fault, so he listed twelve virtues, temperance, silence, order and the rest.

Then a Quaker friend told him people found him proud, so Franklin added a thirteenth: humility. He gave each virtue a page in a little book, with a column for every day of the week, and each slip got a black spot.
The surprise was how many spots there were.

teach.b: He never finished the book clean. But he wrote that he was a better and happier man for trying.
Franklin's little book is a homemade version of something traditions also do: write the way of life down, so you can see where you stand.
Sikhs have the Rahit Maryada, a written code of Sikh conduct that includes daily prayers and how the community lives together.

Buddhists keep the five precepts: not killing, not stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, no intoxicants. They're called training rules, taken on by the person who says them, not commands handed down.
Here's the teaching under all three.

teach.h: A RULE YOU CAN SEE AND KEEP.
teach.b: Written down, a rule stops being a vague good intention. It becomes something you can look at, keep, slip on, and come back to. That's this week in one picture.
Greening, her music, my anthology, read it aloud, my own, a little rule. Each was a line you could carry.
A rule is just those lines, written where you'll see them.

how: The Sikh Rahit Maryada sets out a written code of Sikh conduct; lay Buddhists take on the five precepts by reciting them as training rules; others keep personal rules, as Franklin did with his chart of virtues.

o: rules that people from every faith are required to obey
traditions that write a way of life down to keep it
a list of things forbidden to anyone living alone

p: a slip against one of his virtues
a written code of Sikh conduct

s: Franklin finished his little book with no black spots
he never got it clean, but wrote that trying made him better and happier.
the Buddhist precepts are called training rules, taken on by the one who says them
they're undertaken by the person, not imposed from outside.

games.q: your friend's new year list lives only in her head and has faded by February. she asks why some people bother writing a rule. what fits today?
o: written down, an intention becomes something you can see, slip on and come back to.
writing it down guarantees she'll never slip again.
it doesn't matter; a rule kept in your head works just the same.
games.why: Franklin's spots showed him what he couldn't see; the precepts and the Rahit give a life something to return to.

practice: Count this week's lines on your fingers, one per finger: greening, her music, my anthology, read it aloud, my own, a little rule.
Stop on the one you'd most want written somewhere you'll see it every day, and stay with it until the time is up.

carryVoice: Here's the line: written down, so a good intention becomes something you can see. A week of lines, kept.
